This page goes with **Chapter 15, Creating Contrast Between Sections** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/CreatingContrast.html). Read it there first. The
chapter is short: a form is only audible if its sections **sound different**, and a composer or arranger makes them different by changing
one or more **elements of music**. The book walks through the second movement of Mozart's *Eine kleine Nachtmusik* (a five-part
rondo) and a modern pop song with a reggae section. Here the same method is applied to tunes and pieces already on the site.

## 15.1 The eight elements

The book lists eight things to compare between two sections:

| Element | Ask yourself |
|---|---|
| **Melody** | Is it a new tune, or the old one varied? Smooth or jumpy? (Don't call an ostinato a melody.) |
| **Harmony** | The key and the mode (major or minor); which chords the section starts and ends on |
| **Rhythm** | What is the most common note value in the section? |
| **Timbre** | Which instruments or tone colours? |
| **Texture** | How many voices (vertical), and how active is each (horizontal)? See [Chapter 14](accompaniment-textures.qmd) |
| **Articulation** | Short and clipped (staccato) or long and connected (legato)? |
| **Dynamics** | Loud or soft? |
| **Register** | High, middle or low? |

[Read 15.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/CreatingContrast.html)

A good question for any pair of sections is not "what is different?" but "**which one or two elements carry the contrast?**" Usually
most elements stay the same.

## 15.2 A verse and a chorus: O Susanna

Here are two eight-bar parts of one song from the Tune Library, the verse and the chorus. The notes are the same instrument at the same
tempo, so only melody, harmony, rhythm and articulation can differ (timbre, dynamics and texture would be an arranger's choice).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## One reading

- **Harmony:** the key stays E♭ major, but the chorus *opens* on the IV chord (A♭) instead of the tonic, which is the biggest change
  in the first bar.
- **Rhythm and melody:** the verse is full of a quick dotted figure (a dotted eighth and a sixteenth, "B3/2c/") and moves by step and skip;
  the chorus begins with long, repeated notes (A-A, C-C-C) and only returns to the verse's dotted tune in its second half.
- **Not changed:** key, tempo, register (roughly), instrument. Nothing here can tell you about timbre, dynamics or texture; that would be
  for a recording to show.
:::

## 15.3 A rondo's contrast map: Eine kleine Nachtmusik, II

The book's classic example is the *Romance* of Mozart's *Eine kleine Nachtmusik* (K. 525, second movement), ABACA. The book points to the
elements that change: in B, rhythm (some sixteenth-note runs), texture (all four parts move together) and articulation (staccato
starts); in C, the harmony (it opens in C minor) as well as rhythm, texture and articulation. Play the movement (the
[Classical Themes](../tools/classical-themes.qmd) page has the opening theme, searched under "Nachtmusik"; the book's own
YouTube recording is linked from [its chapter](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/CreatingContrast.html)) and fill in this grid:

| | A (refrain) | B | A | C | A |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harmony (key, mode) | C major | | | | |
| Rhythm (commonest value) | | | | | |
| Texture | | | | | |
| Articulation | | | | | |
| Dynamics | | | | | |
| Register | | | | | |

Which cell is *different from A* in B? In C? Mozart also writes short **transitional** bars to ease from one section into the next
(see [Chapter 25](sonata-rondo.qmd) for the idea of transitions).

For a rondo you can read as well as hear, see
[Beethoven's Op. 49 No. 2, Tempo di Menuetto](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=beethoven-sonata-20-2) in the Analysed Scores Library: its
refrain is in G, with episodes in D and C.

## 15.4 Contrast in a pop song

In the book's pop example, the verse is stripped down (voice and two guitars), then drums and bass come in for verse 2, the pre-chorus goes
legato and the snare drops out, the chorus goes higher in register, and the post-chorus switches to a different rhythm. The **chord
progression barely changes**, so the form is shown almost entirely by texture, articulation, register and rhythm. That is a good thing to
know when you arrange: you can mark a form without changing the chords.

You can hear this on the site. On the [Form in Popular Music](pop-forms.qmd) page the band plays a verse–chorus form as bare chords, so there
is little to tell the sections apart; in the [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd), try the same chart in a quiet style for the verse
and a fuller one for the chorus, and notice what the band does (the Mixer lets you drop the drums or the piano for a section). The
[Arranger](../tools/arranger.qmd) page has intro, main, fill and break sections built on exactly this idea.

## 15.5 Try it

Pick one song you know and write its sections on a timeline (Timestamp Notes keeps it:
[Timestamp Notes](../tools/timestamp-notes.qmd)). For each pair of neighbouring sections, name the **one or two elements that carry the
contrast**. Which sections stay the same in the elements you can't hear in a lead sheet? Then write a short section you could add to it in
which only *one* element changes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **The grid** is the book's method. Which elements change in B and C is summarised from the chapter (checked against its text on
  2026-11-09); the grid is left blank so students listen for the rest.
- **O Susanna:** the two parts are the site's Tune Library version (the recorder teacher's guide). The reading is this page's own, from the notation; it says
  nothing about performance.
- **Not here:** the book's pop example (a copyrighted recording) and the "contrast" quiz the book lacks. A small listening drill is
  possible from the Arranger's styles but has not been built.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
